summaries.gardner: American Express has a famous brand, top customer satisfaction and long-term backing from Berkshire Hathaway, but it is a mature, 170-year-old leader rather than a top dog in an emerging industry, and its shares fell about 5% over the past year. It fits Gardner's Rule Maker idea better than his Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: Amex is a classic Buffett holding: Berkshire has owned it for decades and holds roughly a fifth of the company, drawn by its brand, closed-loop network and 30%-plus return on equity. Results have been consistent and capital is returned through dividends and buybacks, though it relies on borrowed funding as any lender does and the stock is not cheap at about 18-19 times trailing earnings.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the simple, durable model of an affluent card base paying fees and merchants paying a premium to reach it, and Berkshire's long ownership reflects that. Inverting, the main ways it could fail are a credit-card rate cap, a severe credit cycle or banks out-competing it on rewards; none looks fatal, but the price of about 6 times book leaves little margin for error.
summaries.lynch: Amex is a stalwart with a simple story: more spending per card, higher fees and buybacks lift earnings about 10-15% a year. At about 18.6 times trailing earnings against EPS growth of roughly 10-14% (2026 guidance $17.30-$17.90 vs $15.38), the P/E is above the growth rate, so it is fairly priced rather than a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Amex shows several Fisher qualities: long-run sales growth, strong selling and marketing, regular product refreshes (Platinum 2025, Gold 2024) and a highly rated workforce (No. 4 on Fortune's 2026 Best Companies list). It is weaker on R&D-driven innovation and has very heavy marketing and rewards costs that cap margin expansion.
summaries.graham: Amex passes Graham's tests for size, a dividend record stretching back to the 19th century, ten years of profits and strong long-term EPS growth. It fails on price: about 18.6 times trailing earnings and 6 times book value give a P/E times P/B near 112, far above Graham's 22.5 limit, so it is not a defensive-investor bargain.
summaries.thiel: Amex has a quasi-monopoly position in premium charge cards and a closed-loop network built over decades, but its technology is not ten times better than rivals' and the market is contested by Chase, Citi and Capital One. It scores well on distribution and durability and poorly on secrets and timing.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with rising estimates at reasonable prices; Amex compounds EPS at low-to-mid teens and trades near 16.5 times forward earnings, a reasonable price. But it is not a beneficiary of a big platform shift like AI, and regulatory risk from a proposed rate cap makes it a lower-conviction idea for his style.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, rates and earnings momentum; Amex's earnings are growing steadily but not accelerating sharply, and the stock lagged the market over the past year. Rate cuts help its funding costs, but a possible rate cap and consumer-credit risks give no clear macro tailwind.
summaries.smith: Amex fits Terry Smith's 'good company' tests partly: high return on equity (about 34-36%), a strong brand and steady growth. It falls short of his preference for asset-light firms with high gross margins and low leverage, since it is a lender with liabilities about 8 times equity.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Amex's earnings yield is reasonable (operating income about 6.5% of enterprise value), but return on capital is hard to measure for a lender and is middling on invested-capital measures (about 12% ROIC). It is not a clear Magic Formula pick.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool is a good business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high returns; Amex has the first two, with a 30%-plus ROE, a strong brand and long-tenured management. Reinvestment is more limited, since it returns most of its profit through dividends and roughly $8 billion a year of buybacks.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary trouble bought far below value with little downside; Amex is simple and the chance of permanent loss is small, but it is not distressed or deeply discounted. The 2026 rate-cap scare offered only a modest dip.
summaries.wood: Amex is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics, and its market will not multiply in five years. It is more likely to be pressured by digital-wallet and pay-by-bank disruption than to benefit from it.
summaries.ackman: Amex matches several of Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with a dominant brand and high barriers to entry. It is less insulated from outside forces than he prefers, since interest rates, consumer credit and regulation affect it, and Pershing Square does not hold it.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured 'scale economies shared' businesses that pass savings to customers; Amex reinvests heavily in rewards and service for cardholders, but it charges premium prices rather than lowering them as it grows. It is a strong franchise but not a clear scale-economies-shared model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets, painful problems and new technology waves; Amex serves a large, mature payments market, not an emerging one. It is a long-established incumbent rather than the kind of startup opportunity Sequoia sought.
summaries.nash: Amex fails several of Nash's hard filters: as a lender it carries more debt than cash, its operating margin hovers around 19-20%, and its expenses are growing faster than revenue. It does well on moat, talent, ownership and short interest, scores about 75 on his 13 categories, and a simple DCF gives roughly $365 a share, above today's price.

momentum.evidence: AXP closed at $306.95 on October 14, 2026, about 5% lower than a year earlier and below its 50- and 200-day averages, while the S&P 500 was near record highs.

g4.evidence: CEO Stephen Squeri has run Amex since 2018, and Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway is its largest shareholder with a stake of roughly a fifth of the company.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate Amex a Buy with an average target of about $369 (October 2026), and it trades at about 16.5 times forward earnings, so it is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: Amex earns merchant discount fees (52% of 2025 revenue), interest on card loans (24%) and annual card fees (14%), a model a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $36.1 billion in 2020 to $72.2 billion in 2025, and Amex has stayed profitable through recessions, including 2020.

integrity.evidence: Amex gives clear annual guidance (2026 EPS $17.30-$17.90), returns capital through dividends ($1.3 billion) and buybacks ($3.9 billion) in the first half of 2026, and has a long-tenured, stable leadership team.

b6.evidence: Amex sticks to its spend-centric premium card model and makes only small tuck-in acquisitions such as Tock and Rooam rather than empire-building deals.

roic.evidence: Return on equity is very high at 33.9% in 2025 and 36.4% in Q2 2026, but as a lender it relies on deposits and $59 billion of borrowings, and ROIC on all capital is about 12%.

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow was about $15.1 billion against net income of about $11.3 billion, though a lender's cash flow swings with card-loan growth.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded card growth that lifted revenue from $36.1 billion in 2020 to $72.2 billion in 2025 while diluted shares fell from 806 million to 696 million, and market value rose to about $207 billion.

safety.evidence: A simple 12% discount-rate DCF gives about $365 a share versus $306.95, a modest cushion that depends on FCF assumptions for a lender.

fairprice.evidence: About 16.5 times forward earnings for a business with a 34%-plus ROE and about 10% revenue growth is reasonable.

mu5.evidence: The brand and network are durable, but a severe credit downturn, a federal rate cap or losing a big co-brand partner like Delta could seriously hurt results.

reinvest.evidence: Amex can keep growing card fees and lending at high returns on equity, but it returns most profits through dividends and buybacks rather than reinvesting them.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: steady 8-10% growth in card spending plus fees and buybacks driving low-to-mid-teens EPS growth.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 18.6 is above the roughly 10-14% EPS growth rate (2025 EPS $15.38 to 2026 guidance of $17.30-$17.90).

runway.evidence: Amex sees growth from younger customers, international merchant acceptance and small-business services, but it is already a $72 billion revenue company in a mature market.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 806 million in 2020 to 679 million in Q2 2026, but insiders, including CEO Squeri, have been selling rather than buying on the open market.

ly8.evidence: Amex is a widely followed large cap covered by about 30 analysts and famously owned by Berkshire Hathaway.

fi2.evidence: Amex refreshes its flagship products regularly, including the US Gold Card in 2024 and the Platinum Card in 2025, and adds dining services through Resy and Tock.

fi3.evidence: Technology spending supports low fraud and a 2.0% write-off rate and digital products, but Amex does not report R&D and its innovations are incremental.

fi4.evidence: Amex has the most valuable premium card franchise and sells it well: net card fees rose double digits for 30 straight quarters to $10.0 billion in 2025.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps spending heavily on marketing and card refreshes for long-term customer growth even when it weighs on near-term expense growth (expenses up 12% in Q2 2026).

gr1.evidence: Amex had $72.2 billion of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $207 billion in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: Amex has been profitable every year over the last decade, with its lowest recent profit of $3.1 billion in pandemic-hit 2020.

gr4.evidence: Amex has paid dividends without interruption for well over 20 years and raised its quarterly dividend about 16% to $0.95 in 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS reached $15.38 in 2025, roughly four times the $3.77 of 2020 and far more than one third above the levels of ten years earlier.

gr6.evidence: At $306.95 the shares trade at about 18.6 times trailing earnings, above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: With a P/E of about 18.6 and price-to-book of about 6.0, the product is about 112, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Amex's closed-loop network and data are strong, but its technology is not ten times better than Visa, Mastercard or bank issuers'.

timing.evidence: Shifts from cash to cards and growth in younger affluent spenders help, but premium-card competition and a possible rate cap make timing mixed.

th3.evidence: Amex built a dominant share of the premium charge-card niche before expanding into lending, small business, corporate cards and dining services.

team.evidence: Management under Squeri is experienced and has executed well, but it is a strong professional team rather than an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: Amex owns its customer relationships directly as issuer and network, with strong distribution through co-brand partners like Delta, Marriott and Hilton.

durable.evidence: Its brand and network have lasted over a century and should hold, but pay-by-bank, wallets and banks' premium cards could erode its position over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Premium rewards cards are now a well-understood, crowded opportunity that Chase, Citi and Capital One all pursue.

trend.evidence: Amex benefits from the slow shift to card payments but is not a leading beneficiary of AI, cloud or another major platform shift.

dr1.evidence: EPS growth is steady (diluted EPS up 14% in the first half of 2026) and revenue guidance was raised to 10%, but EPS guidance was held at $17.30-$17.90 rather than raised.

dr2.evidence: Platinum refresh fees and buybacks should lift earnings by 2027 (consensus EPS about $20), but this is broadly expected.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates would cut Amex's funding costs, but a slowing economy and the 2026 push for a 10% card-rate cap work against it.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on October 23 and continued Platinum fee repricing are near-term catalysts, but no single large transforming event is in view.

dr7.evidence: Steady but unspectacular growth and regulatory risk make Amex a core holding rather than a high-conviction concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: As a card issuer Amex reports no gross margin; its pricing power shows instead in net card fees rising 18% to $10.0 billion in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $15.1 billion is a yield of about 7.3% on a $207 billion market value, attractive for its quality.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $14.4 billion is about 6.5% of an enterprise value of about $221 billion, reasonable but not high.

pa2.evidence: The 2026 rate-cap scare and higher marketing spending hurt the shares, but these are not a business setback, as revenue still grew 10% in Q2 2026.

pa4.evidence: With a strong brand, a 36% ROE and profits through every recent downturn, permanent loss of capital looks unlikely.

wo1.evidence: Amex is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Card costs do not fall sharply with volume; rewards and marketing costs grow alongside spending.

wo3.evidence: Amex is a payments and lending business and does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its premium payments market is large and mature and will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Amex is insulated from commodity prices, but interest rates, consumer credit and regulation such as a possible rate cap affect it.

ns1.evidence: Amex uses its scale to fund richer rewards but charges rising annual fees (Platinum $895), the opposite of passing scale savings on as lower prices.

ns4.evidence: Amex is likely to remain a premium leader in 10-20 years, but rivals' premium cards and new payment methods make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: Amex makes paying, travel and business spending easier and safer, a real but not severely painful problem.

tn1.evidence: Amex is a 175-year-old payments company benefiting modestly from digital payments, not a company built for a new secular trend like AI or energy.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Amex as a premium card and lending company, and that is what it is becoming; there is no hidden transformation story.

tn3.evidence: Amex is a $207 billion US large cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since 2020 and it is profitable ($10.8 billion in 2025); it misses on cash vs debt ($45.2 billion vs $59.0 billion), which is valid for a lender funding card loans.

tn5.evidence: Borrowings of about $59 billion exceeded cash of about $45 billion at June 30, 2026, as is normal for a card lender.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 10% in 2025 and 10% in Q2 2026, with 2026 growth guided to about 10%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 10% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 21% gives about 31, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 10% while total expenses grew 11%, and in Q2 2026 revenue grew 10% while expenses grew 12%.

tn9.evidence: It trips the more-debt-than-cash kill ($59.0 billion vs $45.2 billion) and its 2025 operating margin was 19.1%, just under 20%.

tn10.evidence: The January 2026 push for a 10% cap on credit-card interest rates and ongoing merchant-fee legislation and litigation are material regulatory threats.

tn11.evidence: Amex provides premium payment cards and a closed-loop network that help affluent consumers and businesses spend with rewards, service and travel perks, and charges merchant fees, annual card fees and interest.

tn13.evidence: Total about 75: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 5, short interest (about 2%) 10, institutional ownership (about 65%) 10, revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 500 5, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 10; borderline.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025, but margins did not expand steadily and borrowings exceeded cash.

tn15.evidence: 2025 pretax income of $13.8 billion covers interest expense of $8.2 billion only about 1.7 times, and liabilities ($273.9 billion) are about 8 times equity ($34.3 billion).

tn18.evidence: Squeri has executed well since 2018 (revenue doubled from 2020 to 2025), but he has not bought shares in the open market and has not held the role for 10 years.

tn20.evidence: Amex usually beats EPS estimates, including Q2 2026, but revenue fell short of forecasts that quarter.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, fraud suspicion or acquisition spree, but expenses are growing faster than revenue and executives, including the CEO, have sold shares.

tn22.evidence: Amex has $72 billion of revenue and $10.8 billion of profit and shrinks its share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 18.6 times trailing earnings and a 7% FCF yield, the price implies growth below the roughly 10% revenue and 14% EPS growth Amex delivered in the first half of 2026.

tn25.evidence: Using trailing FCF of about $15.1 billion, about 11% growth, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, less net debt of about $13.8 billion, value is about $365 a share versus $306.95.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 16.5 is in line with or below card peers, but the PEG is about 1.2-1.3, above 1.
